svg.title: The three steps of the enterprise architecture method in fixed order, the four stakeholder groups to align, and why the order cannot be reversed
svg.desc: Three boxes run left to right: identify business requirements, align stakeholders and identify the operating model. The four stakeholder groups are listed beneath: the IT steering committee with the architecture management office, the vendor-neutral team and senior management; architects, both business and technology and enterprise; finance and procurement with the CFO, procurement and supplier relationships; and enterprise process owners with functional owners, user groups and business unit leaders. A red band states that reversing the order, fixing the operating model first and hunting for requirements afterwards, is the bottom-up error chapter 1 criticised, and that the vendor-neutral team exists to keep vendor lock-in out of the design.
svg.text: Three steps, one order: requirements, then people, then the operating model
Each step constrains the next; nothing downstream can repair an upstream mistake
which outcome, whose problem, by when
four groups, four different definitions of done
output: agreement on the constraint set
two questions place you in one of four quadrants
output: the scope of later standardisation
WHO HAS TO AGREE — AND WHAT EACH GROUP ACTUALLY CARES ABOUT
Step 3 cannot come first. Fix the operating model first and hunt for requirements afterwards and you have the bottom-up error chapter 1 rejected.
The vendor-neutral team in step 2 exists for one reason: to keep vendor lock-in from being designed in.
A framework earns its keep here: it forces these three conversations in this order, before anyone opens a product datasheet.
